lha-7.t: How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sa…
lha-7.tx:
How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sailed wooden boats straight into the deadliest minefield on earth to clear the way for the American fleet?

In February 1991, Iraqi mines tore holes in the amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton. Over one thousand mines still choked the waters off Kuwait.

Western television commentators mocked Japan for only sending money during the war. Those commentators stopped laughing when Captain Taosa Ochiai and six Japanese naval vessels steamed eight thousand miles into the blazing summer heat of the Persian Gulf.

Why did Japan send four tiny wooden-hulled minesweepers, Hikoshima, Yurishima, Awashima, and Sakushima, instead of steel destroyers? Because Iraq had planted Italian-made Manta bottom mines on the seafloor that detonated the instant they sensed the magnetic field or engine hum of a steel hull.

Only non-magnetic hulls built of timber could float over them without blowing up.

Working in 120-degree heat alongside the U.S. Navy, Japanese minesweepers took on the most dangerous shallow sectors where sunken oil tankers and deadly Manta mines waited.

When sonar spotted a mine on the bottom that mechanical cables could not cut, Japanese explosive ordnance divers strapped on flippers, swam down into the murky water by hand, and placed explosive charges right next to live warheads.

Across ninety-nine straight days under the desert sun, Japan's wooden boats destroyed thirty-four deadly mines without losing a single sailor.

On their final day in the Gulf, U.S. Navy commanders stood at attention and saluted the sunburned Japanese crews who had cleared the sea in silence.

Real allies do not boast on television. They take the deadliest sector and clear the path for their friends.

lha-7.tx:
SAILORS FIRST SUNDAY: Sailor Of The Week ⚓

Congratulations to HM2 Brandon W. Williams, a Colorado native who serves as the SAR Medical Technician Standardization Leading Petty Officer (LPO) with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron Two-Five (HSC-25) in Agana, Guam!

As medical department LPO, he led five HMs and advised one Senior Medical Officer in FDNF command medical readiness, pre/post deployment medical requirements, and medical training for 435 sailors from HSC-25, AIMD, ASD, AIMD Bahrain, VUP-19, and ERCS Naval Hospital Guam. 

His leadership resulted in treating 560 patients, inoculating 125 service members from Influenza, Japanese Encephalitis and Hepatitis, 18 flight physicals, 109 post-deployment health assessments and 53 pre-deployment health screenings, contributing to 92% squadron medical readiness, as well as the deployment of Detachment 3 and Detachment 6 in support of ESB-6/ LHA-7.

As a Search and Rescue Medical Technician, Williams responded directly to two Medevacs, including one stroke patient that required urgent intervention to prevent neurological deterioration and one renal failure patient that required higher-level care, impacting two souls saved. As Command Tactical Combat Casualty Care Program Director, his instruction has qualified 73 personnel in TCCC tier 2, as well as 19 enlisted in TCCC All Service Member. 

His professionalism, leadership, and unwavering commitment exemplify the standards expected of our Navy’s finest Sailors!

cvn-71.t: A multibillion-rupee F-35C fighter jet attempted to land on the USS Theodore Roosevelt but failed to catch an arresting cable, forcing the pilot to take off ag…
cvn-71.tx:
A multibillion-rupee F-35C fighter jet attempted to land on the USS Theodore Roosevelt but failed to catch an arresting cable, forcing the pilot to take off again. The footage reportedly shows an F/A-18F Super Hornet landing successfully before the F-35C’s unsuccessful attempt.

Aircraft carriers use arresting cables stretched across the flight deck. A fighter jet’s tailhook must catch one of these cables to bring the aircraft to a stop within the short landing area. If the hook misses every cable, the pilot must immediately power up and climb away.

This is known as a “bolter.” It is a recognised part of carrier aviation, not necessarily a sign of aircraft malfunction. With a short deck, tight timing and little room for error, carrier landings remain among the most demanding operations in military aviation.

cvn-76.tx:
When a military transport plane crashes into the open ocean five hundred miles from land, the difference between life and death is measured in the first forty minutes.

On the afternoon of November 22, 2017, a U.S. Navy C-2A Greyhound carrying eleven sailors lost power and slammed into the Philippine Sea while flying toward the aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan.

In the middle of the vast Pacific, waiting hours for search planes usually means nobody comes home.

Why did help arrive from the sky and sea in less than forty minutes? Because at that exact moment, warships and helicopters of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, including the destroyer JS Ikazuchi, were sailing side by side with the Ronald Reagan in a joint alliance exercise.

The moment the distress beacon flashed, Japanese and American commanders did not need translators or bureaucratic permission. They had trained together on the same frequencies for years.

Japanese destroyers immediately wheeled hard into the waves at flank speed while U.S. Navy and Japanese SH-60K helicopters launched straight toward the smoke marker.

Rescue swimmers leaped into the churning swells and pulled eight surviving American sailors from the water in forty minutes flat, flying them straight back to the flight deck of the Ronald Reagan alive.

For the next two days and nights, eight U.S. and Japanese warships searched grid by grid side by side for the three fallen brothers.

An alliance is not a piece of paper signed in Washington or Tokyo. It is a Japanese destroyer turning full speed toward an American flare in the middle of the sea.

al-dhafra.t: 🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipm…
al-dhafra.tx:
🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran

The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipment, is a key node in the network of US and allied air operations in the Persian Gulf. This base was targeted 159 times during the Iran-Iraq War (Ramadan War).

The equipment stationed at this base connected reconnaissance, information transmission, command, and air operation support elements; a system that can be described as the "eyes, brain, and arm of air operations."

Information from the base's radars and reconnaissance aircraft was combined to create a common picture of the regional situation, which was then provided to the Al Udeid air operations center. Communication centers and satellite data reception facilities also served as a link for transmitting this information to commanders and operational units.

In the operational section, the 380th Air Expeditionary Wing managed missions related to reconnaissance aircraft, fighter jets, tankers, and air support. Large fuel storage tanks and aircraft maintenance facilities also provided the necessary support for the continuity of these missions.

The presence of US, UAE, and French forces gave Al Dhafra a multinational status, making it one of the key points for connecting the air power of these countries in the region.

The diversity of these targets indicates that in the attacks, in addition to aircraft, the necessary infrastructure for detection, reconnaissance, data transmission, command, and the continuation of operations was also a target. However, the targeting of each of these facilities, in itself, does not necessarily indicate the extent of the damage or its removal from the operational cycle.

The operational consequence highlighted in this account is the transformation of Al Dhafra from a support base into a point vulnerable to repeated attacks. This situation forces the US to allocate part of its capabilities and resources to protecting the base, dispersing equipment, and maintaining communication between the components of the network.

Farsna

This development serves as context for everything else happening today. Keep this at forefront as we examine events unfolding below.

Riyadh reports two powerful explosions. Saudi Civil Defense had issued aerial threat warning just before blasts. Jeddah reports explosions; cause and extent of damage remain undisclosed. Dammam reports flight operations at King Fahd International Airport have been suspended.

India Akasa Air has suspended all flights to and from Riyadh until 30 November 2026. This is no mere temporary adjustment. This is airline voting with own capital: skies over Riyadh are unsafe, so they are ceasing operations for over month.

Saudi airports are appearing on suspended operations list one after another. Saudi Civil Defense is issuing warnings ahead of explosions. Sirens are sounding in Saudi capital.

Four airstrikes hit Harf Sufyan district of Amran Governorate. Two hit Khayar area of Bani Sarim district. Three hit Taiziyah district of Taiz. Four hit across Sahar and Majz districts of Saada. Another four hit Al-Salem area of Saada. In Al-Munqam village of Al-Durayhimi district in Hodeidah, civilian farm was struck, resulting in death of several livestock. Al-Mokha port received one to three strikes. Nihm District, Sanaa received series of airstrikes, resulting in 12 casualties, dead and wounded. Harad District, Hajjah received one strike. Shada border district, Saada received artillery shelling. East of Saada city received missile attack.

In Al-Aqrudh, Al-Misrakh District, Taiz, home of Khalid Abdu Hassan was struck. Woman and two children were killed. Six others were wounded.

This is what Saudi Arabia did on very same day that airports remained closed, capital was under bombardment, and airlines had been grounded for over month. It bombed livestock on farm. It bombed port. It bombed water utility building. It bombed family.

Army that cannot win on battlefield is left with nothing but to bomb such targets. This is not strategy. This is incompetence, incompetence masked by blood of Yemeni people.

Ansarallah has seized Harir and Al-Nabik defensive lines on Lahj front, advancing toward Shateen Valley. Forces are currently clearing high ground that leads toward Aden.

This is not mere harassment. This is advance. Lahj serves as northern gateway to Aden, with Harir and Al-Nabik acting as its key defensive anchors. With these anchors removed, road to Aden lies open.

Today, Saudi backed forces in Aden were struck by drones, coinciding with collapse of defensive lines in Lahj.

Saudi Arabia entire ground presence in southern Yemen is being squeezed from north.

muwaffaq-salti.t: 🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Iran hit 274 buildings on 24 US bases in six months and aimed for the barracks where troops sleep, and the Pentagon still won't say what it cost What the…
muwaffaq-salti.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Iran hit 274 buildings on 24 US bases in six months and aimed for the barracks where troops sleep, and the Pentagon still won't say what it cost

What the Wall Street Journal found in tens of thousands of satellite images:

-274 damaged structures at 24 installations across Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iraq in the war's first six months

-119 buildings hit in the first two weeks alone, most of them in Kuwait; the Fifth Fleet's base in Bahrain was largely evacuated

-After the ceasefire collapsed in July, Iran shifted fire west to Jordan and hit buildings half the size of its earlier targets, matching housing units; the July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti killed 3 Americans and damaged 19 barracks

-Iranian media claims of strikes on troop housing doubled in that stretch; the Journal found damage to housing at three more bases the same week

-More than 20 US service members dead and 400-plus wounded before the Pentagon stopped publishing war-specific casualty figures in July

-Base damage priced at a minimum of $5 billion and possibly $15 billion, on top of the $47.1 billion war bill; CSIS puts rebuilding alone above $4 billion

-Hegseth declared Iran's missile program "functionally defeated" on March 13 and Trump said its missiles were "just about used up" on April 1; Iran kept hitting bases for five more months

-Sen. Murphy was barred from visiting Al Udeid, where at least a dozen buildings show damage, and says the Pentagon is "withholding information" to hide the war's cost

Hegseth's story and the satellite record don't match, and the gap is the problem for next week. 

The Pentagon moved troops off bases and is now talking about pulling back from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia entirely, which is what you do when you expect the next round to hit harder, and officials admit Iran has saved its best missiles.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

The mission is working, and that's the best argument against a strike: oil is flowing, Iran's economy is collapsing, so hold the line indefinitely.

The catch is the people doing the holding.

Every month adds $2 to $3 billion, more worn-out jets and longer stretches away from home for crews who were promised relief, and the White House now has to decide whether the next week brings a short, intense campaign or tells those sailors the blockade is their job for the foreseeable future.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

October 24, 2026. Central Iran. Footage of a missile test has emerged. Based on the ballistic trajectory, this appears to be a new type of ballistic missile system undergoing operational testing.

💥 This is not merely a "test launch," it is an "acceptance test prior to delivery."

As IRGC spokesperson Mohebbi previously stated, Iran’s missile stockpile has increased by 150%, with significant improvements in quality including greater range, higher precision, and enhanced destructive power. "Should the war escalate, surprises will be revealed."

These tests represent the first installment of those "surprises."

🎯 The Timing of the Tests

Russia has just confirmed that its personnel have not been evacuated from the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. Russian nuclear experts and diplomats remain on-site, signaling to Washington and Tel Aviv: you may issue threats, but those threats will not force our withdrawal.

On the same day, Iran conducts tests of a new missile system. This is no coincidence; it is a dual-track signal, Russia’s deterrent presence at Bushehr, combined with Iran’s missile capabilities in its interior.

📜 What Is This System?

Based on its ballistic profile, this appears to be a two-stage, solid-fuel system equipped with a maneuverable re-entry vehicle (MaRV). Solid-fuel propulsion eliminates the need for on-site fueling or lengthy preparation, allowing for launch within minutes of leaving storage. The MaRV capability enables the warhead to alter its trajectory during the terminal phase, effectively thwarting the predictive calculations of interceptor systems.

This is not just an increase in quantity; it is a qualitative leap. The system’s range covers Israel, U.S. military bases in Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia, as well as the U.S. facility on Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

⚔️ The Location of the Tests

The tests took place in Central Iran not near the borders or the coast, but deep within the country’s interior. This means the launch sites are situated far from the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf coastline, protected by layers of air defense systems and positioned well beyond the operational radius of U.S. carrier strike groups.

A missile launched from the interior is far more difficult to destroy in a preemptive strike than one launched from the coast. 

🔻 The Ledger

The United States has spent $11 billion on missile defense for Israel, firing 609 interceptors. Now, Iran is testing new systems.

This is not an "arms race." It is "cost imposition." The cost of a single interceptor is dozens of times higher than that of an offensive missile. Every time the U.S. intercepts one, it loses money. Every time Iran tests a new system, it drives up the cost of U.S. interception.

A nation that can still test new missile systems in the eighth month of a war is not collapsing. It is declaring: My production lines are running. My engineers are innovating. My missiles are taking flight.

diego-garcia.tx:
Fact check if the nonsense spoken by @RaheemKassam about @KemiBadenoch with @lewis_goodall on @LBC.

Claim: Kemi Badenoch lied about what Nigel Farage said about the Chagos Islands.

False

Explanation: Nigel Farage proposed "gifting" full control of the military base at Diego Garcia to Donald Trump as part of a geopolitical trade. 

During an appearance on The Benny Show podcast, Farage pitched a hypothetical deal:

"I'd have gone in and said, 'Right, you know what, mate? Chagos, it's yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world... In return, just please stop talking about the Falkland Islands.'"

Claim: Kemi Badenoch has championed DEI in government.

False

Explanation: Kemi Badenoch is widely known as a fierce critic of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) policies, often campaigning against identity politics and public sector equality duties rather than championing them.

Claim: Badenoch has lied about her position on the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

False

Explanation: While political opponents have debated her stance, Badenoch's actual position during her leadership campaign was to criticize rivals who promised immediate withdrawal from the ECHR, describing those promises as offering "easy answers" rather than a straightforward lie about her own policy.

Badenoch has since concluded that reforming the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) from within is no longer viable and that the UK must withdraw from the agreement. She announced that leaving the ECHR and repealing the Human Rights Act will be explicit manifesto pledges for the Conservative Party to ensure the UK can deport foreign criminals and control its borders without legal intervention.

Claim: She lied about her Stanford scholarship.

False

Explanation: Badenoch previously stated that at age 16, her SAT scores earned her a partial scholarship offer to study a "pre-med" course at Stanford University, which her family ultimately could not afford.

Referring to taking a science undergraduate degree as "pre-med" is a common colloquialism in the US that Kemi Badenoch adopted from her time spent living in America.

Claim: She said on LBC, "I was a—I was a Muslim, I was born in a country that was 50% Muslim."

False (Misquoted/Inaccurate context)

Explanation: In discussions regarding her background and family, Badenoch has noted that her grandmother was a Muslim or that she grew up in Nigeria (which has a roughly split Muslim/Christian population), but she did not state that she herself was a practicing Muslim in the way quoted.

Claim: She lied about her meeting with Meloni.

False

Explanation: The narrative that Giorgia Meloni warned Kemi Badenoch against doing business with Reform UK stemmed from media reporting—most notably initial reports by The Times—rather than official briefings from Badenoch or Conservative Campaign Headquarters. Conservative spokespeople consistently maintained that neither Badenoch nor the party made any false claims, attributing the misunderstanding to media interpretation and political sensationalism by rivals.

akrotiri.t: UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll —— According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Min…
akrotiri.tx:
UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll
——
According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Ministry of Defense (MoD) has expanded its military assistance to Saudi Arabia, deploying Royal Air Force (RAF) Typhoon fighter jets and providing critical aerial refueling for Saudi airstrikes targeting Yemen.

The increased support was authorized by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, who previously advocated for an arms embargo against Riyadh over its civilian casualty record in Yemen, but is now presiding over direct British involvement as Saudi strikes hit civilian centers.

Data from the Yemen Data Project reveals that Saudi airstrikes caused more civilian casualties last month than in any single period since 2022, resulting in at least 66 deaths and 90 injuries—including eight children.

Among the deadliest incidents was a September 22 strike on a residential home in Mokha that killed six civilians, followed days later by an attack on a market in the Al-Taiziyah district of Taiz that killed seven and injured 40 others.

Despite the rising toll, London agreed to send up to 20 Voyager aerial refueling sorties from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus with their transponders deactivated, while deploying Typhoons from Qatar to support Saudi air operations without charging the kingdom for the military assistance.

The escalation follows the collapse of a four-year UN-brokered ceasefire in July, triggered when Saudi-led forces bombed Sanaa International Airport. In response to the breakdown, Yemen's Armed Forces have launched retaliatory drone and missile strikes against strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

While ten leading British trade unions and human rights monitors have demanded an immediate halt to UK military collaboration, British officials maintain that RAF deployments serve strictly "defensive counter air" purposes to protect regional allies.

#Tehran has issued a pointed warning to Berlin, declaring that #German military bases and associated facilities throughout the #MiddleEast would be treated as legitimate targets should Germany openly participate in any military operation against Iran, according to a report from the #IRGC-linked Fars News Agency.
The message, conveyed amid rising regional tensions, follows what Iranian sources describe as an escalation of “anti-Iranian measures” by Germany. It also includes demands that Berlin end what Tehran calls the harassment of Iranian residents in Germany based on what it terms baseless accusations—a reference tied to recent German legal actions against individuals linked to Iranian intelligence.
#Iranian officials and media have simultaneously signaled that a new round of direct conflict is viewed as increasingly probable. In the weeks leading up to the warning, Iran has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests, which observers interpret as part of broader preparations and efforts to demonstrate remaining strike capabilities despite earlier damage to its arsenal and production infrastructure.
Potential targets highlighted in the warning focus on German-linked military infrastructure in the wider region. While Germany maintains a comparatively limited permanent footprint in the Middle East relative to the United States or #UnitedKingdom, the statement broadly covers any barracks, bases, or facilities associated with German forces or operations. Related reporting in recent weeks has also drawn attention to concerns over U.S. installations on German soil (such as Ramstein and Spangdahlem), which serve as major logistics and command hubs supporting regional missions, though the Fars warning specifically addresses German assets across the region rather than on German territory itself.
This development occurs against a backdrop of ongoing friction, including German diplomatic summons of Iranian representatives and judicial outcomes involving alleged plots, as Tehran positions itself for possible renewed hostilities.

fairford.tx:
NEW: Staggering details emerging from Westminster Mags on the RAF Fairford plot today.

One of the five men arrested near the US military base called the police after a "handler" warned there was a bomb in the van, a court heard.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.

Abdulkarim, of London, is accused of assisting a foreign intelligence service, by acting as an “intermediary” for the handler Ali.

While Essghir, also of London, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, relating to an alleged “reconnaissance” mission on August 22, around a month before the Fairford incident.

The group were ordered to drive the van loaded with petrol to RAF Fairford by a handler known as ‘Ali’ who police believe was working on behalf of Iran.

No explosives, or improvised explosives were found in the vans, the court heard.

Police did find a metal oil drum in each, two of which had petrol in, along with hard plastic water butts and internet-enabled dashcams.

Prosecuting, Louise Gray, said: “Shortly thereafter the message was received that there was a bomb in the vehicles and one of them called the police.”

Abdulkarim is alleged to have aided the organiser, Ali, who is believed to be abroad and to be acting in the interests of the Iranian state.

Ali is also potentially connected to an incident at the Israeli embassy earlier this year, where propaganda videos were posted online suggesting it had been attacked with a chemical weapon by a drone, the court heard.

Prosecutors allege that Abdulkarim aided Ali, buying equipment for the mission and receiving multiple payments from him totalling around £70,000.

Before the men, allegedly enlisted by Abdulkarim, travelled to RAF Fairford, £300 worth of petrol was filled into the drums in the back of the vans.

The U.S. Air Force trained with Zone 5 Technologies’ Paladin counter-drone multirotor at MacDill Air Force Base, Florida, on October 8, 2026, alongside Joint Interagency Task Force 401.

The six-rotor drone was equipped with a Gen12 launcher designed to fire net rounds that entangle the rotors of hostile drones, bringing them down without using conventional ammunition or explosives.

The training provided personnel with another option for protecting military installations and critical infrastructure. The Air Force has not disclosed whether live interceptions were conducted or whether it plans to procure the system.

MacDill AFB hosts the headquarters of U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command, as well as the 6th Air Refueling Wing.

macdill.t: The U.S. Air Force is training with the Bumblebee V2 drone interceptor at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida to strengthen air base protection against small unm…
macdill.tx:
The U.S. Air Force is training with the Bumblebee V2 drone interceptor at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida to strengthen air base protection against small unmanned aircraft, Army Recognition reported.

Personnel from the 6th Security Forces Squadron trained with Joint Interagency Task Force 401 on October 8, 2026. The system, from the U.S. company Perennial Autonomy, is a first-person-view multirotor designed to collide with hostile drones, rendering both inoperable without an explosive warhead. A $5.2 million agreement was awarded to the company on January 30, 2026, for military assessment, with deliveries beginning in March.

The training also included the Paladin system, which uses a net round. Bumblebee V2 features automated target recognition and multi-camera setups from earlier Army tests at Fort Bragg and Fort Benning. The activity supports developing procedures that combine electronic countermeasures with physical interceptors for installation defense. The release confirms training but does not establish permanent deployment or a successful interception at the base.

pearl-harbor.t: The worst battleship of WW2 might be Japan's Fuso. A ship so badly designed that its own navy kept it out of the fight for almost the entire war, and then sent…
pearl-harbor.tx:
The worst battleship of WW2 might be Japan's Fuso. A ship so badly designed that its own navy kept it out of the fight for almost the entire war, and then sent it to die in the last battleship duel in history.

When Fuso was completed in 1915, she was briefly one of the most powerful battleships in the world. Twelve 14-inch guns. Japan's first true super-dreadnought.

But the designers made a fatal choice. They spread those twelve guns across six turrets, running almost the whole length of the ship. Two at the front, two in the middle, two at the back.

That meant six separate ammunition magazines scattered along the hull. Huge stretches of the ship had to be armored to protect explosives. The armor couldn't cover all of it well. And when the middle turrets fired, the blast interfered with the rest of the ship.

Then in the 1930s, Japan modernized her. They gave her new engines, more armor, and a towering "pagoda" mast. It rose so high above the deck it looked like it might tip her over. It became one of the strangest silhouettes of any warship ever built.

By WW2, Fuso was old, slow, and fragile. The Japanese Navy knew it.

So when the war started, she mostly sat in home waters. She trained crews. She escorted. She waited. During the biggest naval battles of 1942 and 1943, she barely saw action. Japan even considered cutting off her rear turrets and turning her into a half-carrier, then dropped the idea.

Then came October 1944. Leyte Gulf.

Japan was throwing everything it had at the American landings in the Philippines. Fuso and her near-sister Yamashiro were assigned to Admiral Shoji Nishimura's Southern Force. Their job was to push through Surigao Strait at night and hit the landing beaches.

The Americans were waiting.

At the far end of the strait sat six US battleships, plus cruisers, destroyers, and torpedo boats. Five of those six battleships had been at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Some had been sunk in the mud that day, raised, and rebuilt.

They had come back for revenge.

Early on October 25, 1944, American destroyers charged down the strait in the dark and fired torpedoes. At least one slammed into Fuso around 3 a.m. Fires spread. She fell out of line.

For decades, the story was that Fuso blew up and broke in two, with both burning halves drifting in the strait while the battle raged around them. It's in countless books.

But when her wreck was finally found and surveyed in 2017, it raised real doubts about that story. The truth of her last minutes is still being argued.

What isn't in doubt is how it ended. Fuso went down with nearly her entire crew. Over 1,500 men. Only a handful are believed to have survived.

Minutes later, Yamashiro steamed straight into the American battle line. The US battleships crossed her T and opened fire. Yamashiro was torn apart and sank with Admiral Nishimura aboard.

It was the last time in history that battleships fought battleships.

Fuso spent almost the whole war being kept away from combat because her navy knew what she was. When they finally sent her in, she didn't survive the night.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane. She was just 22. If you’ve seen Tora! Tor…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane.

She was just 22.

If you’ve seen Tora! Tora! Tora! (1970), you may remember the civilian flight instructor suddenly surrounded by Japanese aircraft.

Her name was Cornelia Fort, a strikingly beautiful young woman and a skilled pilot. The woman behind that scene was real.

On December 7, 1941, Cornelia was giving a flying lesson over Oahu when a Japanese Zero came dangerously close. She seized the controls and narrowly avoided a collision.

Then she saw smoke rising over Pearl Harbor.

Cornelia brought her student safely back to the airfield. She had become one of the few American pilots to witness the opening attack from the air.

In September 1942, she joined the Women’s Auxiliary Ferrying Squadron, becoming one of the pioneering women entrusted with flying military aircraft across the United States. They served as civilians, delivering planes needed for the war effort.

On March 21, 1943, another aircraft struck the BT-13 she was ferrying over Texas. Fort’s aircraft crashed, killing her. She became the first American woman pilot to die in the line of duty flying for the U.S. military.

She was 24.

Hollywood preserved a moment of her life. Her name deserves to be remembered, too.

See the first post for real photos of Cornelia.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸 On July 4, 1944, a tabby kitten named Princess Papule, affectionately known as Pooli, was reportedly born at the Pearl Harbor Navy Yard in Hawaii. During Wo…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸 On July 4, 1944, a tabby kitten named Princess Papule, affectionately known as Pooli, was reportedly born at the Pearl Harbor Navy Yard in Hawaii.

During World War II, a sailor named James Lynch brought her aboard the USS Fremont, an American attack transport serving in the Pacific.

Pooli accompanied the crew through major wartime operations, including the campaigns in Palau, the Philippines, and Iwo Jima.

Despite her distinguished record, Pooli reportedly preferred hiding among mailbags whenever the ship’s battle alarm sounded.

Her wartime service was commemorated with three service ribbons and four battle stars displayed on her miniature naval uniform.

After the war, Pooli settled into a peaceful retirement in California.

On July 4, 1959, she celebrated her 15th birthday, and the Los Angeles Times published a remarkable photograph of her wearing her old naval uniform.

By then, Pooli had lost her hearing and most of her teeth, but she was still remembered as a veteran of the Pacific War.

A small cat who once traveled through the dangers of war had lived long enough to celebrate her 15th birthday in peace.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor? The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor?

The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise into one of aviation cinema’s most memorable encounters: two F-14 Tomcats facing Japanese Zero fighters.

Transported back to December 1941, USS Nimitz carries enough firepower to change the course of the Pacific War. Captain Matthew Yelland, played by Kirk Douglas, faces a question no commander’s training could prepare him for: should he intervene?

Then comes the order: “Splash the Zeros.”

Six years before Top Gun, the Tomcat was already a movie star. Real Navy aircrews from VF-84 (the Jolly Rogers) flew the F-14s, while modified T-6 Texans portrayed the Japanese fighters.

Behind the fantasy was demanding aerial choreography: fast jets, much slower propeller aircraft, and camera crews trying to capture both in the same frame. A B-25 camera aircraft eventually helped make the aerial choreography work.

The scene delivers the spectacle. The premise leaves you with the question.

If you commanded USS Nimitz (CVN-68), would you change history?

pearl-harbor.t: Oct 25, 1944. The last time battleships ever fought each other. Japan's plan at Leyte Gulf called for a pincer. While Kurita's main force came from the north,…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Oct 25, 1944. The last time battleships ever fought each other.

Japan's plan at Leyte Gulf called for a pincer. While Kurita's main force came from the north, a smaller force under Vice Admiral Shoji Nishimura would push up through Surigao Strait from the south and fall on the American landing ships at dawn.

Nishimura had two old battleships, Yamashiro and Fuso, a heavy cruiser and four destroyers.

Waiting for him at the top of the strait was Rear Admiral Jesse Oldendorf with six American battleships. Most of them were survivors of Pearl Harbor. West Virginia and California had been sunk there and raised from the mud.

Oldendorf laid a trap. He lined his battleships up across the northern end of the strait, put cruisers on each side, and stationed destroyers and PT boats along the way in.

Late on the night of Oct 24, Nishimura sailed into it.

First came the PT boats, dozens of them, darting in with torpedoes. Then the destroyers, racing down both sides of the strait in the dark. Their torpedoes tore into the Japanese column. Fuso was hit, exploded and burned. Three Japanese destroyers were sunk or crippled.

Nishimura kept coming anyway.

At about 3:50 a.m., the American battleships opened fire. Oldendorf had done what every admiral dreamed of and almost none ever achieved. He had crossed the T. His whole battle line could fire broadsides at the head of the Japanese column, while the Japanese could only fire back with their forward guns.

The radar-directed guns of West Virginia, California and Tennessee smashed Yamashiro. Burning and wrecked, she turned away. At about 4:19 a.m. she capsized and sank, taking Nishimura and almost her entire crew with her.

Of Nishimura's seven ships, only the destroyer Shigure escaped.

A second Japanese force under Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima came up the strait behind him, found burning wreckage everywhere, and turned around.

It was the end of an era. Battleships would never again fight battleships. And the ships that ended that era were old wrecks from Pearl Harbor, finishing what had started there three years earlier.

yokosuka.t: When a young American sailor aboard the nuclear cruiser USS California was dying of a bursting appendix far out in the Pacific Ocean, he was hundreds of miles…
yokosuka.tx:
When a young American sailor aboard the nuclear cruiser USS California was dying of a bursting appendix far out in the Pacific Ocean, he was hundreds of miles beyond the reach of any U.S. Navy helicopter.

Fire Controlman Third Class David Henderson needed surgery fast. A ruptured appendix in rough ocean swells can kill a young sailor long before a warship can steam back to port.

The U.S. Seventh Fleet called their allies in the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force. Within minutes, Japan scrambled four aircraft: a P-3C Orion, an HSS-2B helicopter, and two giant four-engine Shin Meiwa US-1A amphibious flying boats.

Standard military transports need a concrete runway. Japan's US-1A flying boat was engineered to land directly on open ocean waves up to ten feet high.

While the American nuclear cruiser held position in the swells, the orange-and-white Japanese seaplane dropped out of the sky, landed directly on the open Pacific, and taxied right up beside the USS California.

Crews transferred Petty Officer Henderson across the waves by boat into the Japanese seaplane. The Japanese pilots gunned all four turboprop engines, lifted off the water, and rushed him to Atsugi and U.S. Naval Hospital Yokosuka in time for surgery.

It was the first open-ocean seaplane transfer in U.S.-Japan history, all for one young American sailor.

yokosuka.t: For seventy years after World War II, the law was one-sided: if an enemy attacked Japan, American sailors were sworn to die defending her, but if an American s…
yokosuka.tx:
For seventy years after World War II, the law was one-sided: if an enemy attacked Japan, American sailors were sworn to die defending her, but if an American ship was attacked right next to a Japanese warship, Japanese sailors were legally forbidden to defend their American friends.

Prime Minister Shinzo Abe refused to accept that shame any longer.

Despite screaming protesters outside the parliament building in Tokyo, Abe passed historic security laws so Japan could finally stand shoulder to shoulder with the United States.

On May 1, 2017, as North Korea threatened missile strikes across the Pacific, that promise became steel on the water.

Why did Japan send its largest warship, the 814-foot helicopter destroyer JS Izumo, to guard the U.S. Navy ship USNS Richard E. Byrd? Because the Byrd was a vital ammunition and cargo supply vessel crewed mostly by American civilian mariners, steaming south from Yokosuka to resupply the USS Carl Vinson carrier strike group.

Without heavily armed escorts, a supply ship is the most vulnerable target at sea.

As the American supply ship cleared Tokyo Bay, the massive gray flat-top JS Izumo pulled alongside her port beam, launching SH-60K anti-submarine helicopters overhead to sweep the waters all the way to Shikoku.

American sailors watching from the bridge knew what they were seeing. For the first time in postwar history, the Rising Sun flag was sailing as an armed bodyguard for the Stars and Stripes.

A true friend does not hide behind your shield forever. One day, he steps up and locks his shield with yours.

yokosuka.t: If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty…
yokosuka.tx:
If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty. They will point to two thousand Japanese master craftsmen in hard hats waiting inside a 150-year-old stone dry dock.

Keeping the U.S. Seventh Fleet ready to deter conflict across the Indo-Pacific requires constant, grueling hull and combat-system repairs.

Why does the United States Navy not simply sail its damaged or aging warships back to Pearl Harbor or San Diego for maintenance? Because steaming five thousand miles back across the Pacific pulls a frontline warship off patrol for months when every day counts.

Inside Fleet Activities Yokosuka sits Dry Dock Number 1, built out of hand-cut granite stone blocks by Japanese stonemasons in 1871. More than a century and a half later, those ancient stone walls still hold the weight of billion-dollar American Aegis destroyers without cracking an inch.

Working inside those six dry docks is the U.S. Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Center, powered by over two thousand Japanese master welders, pipefitters, shipwrights, and electrical engineers.

Many of these Japanese artisans are second- and third-generation craftsmen whose fathers and grandfathers repaired American warships in the exact same docks.

When the U.S. Seventh Fleet flagship USS Blue Ridge, the oldest operational warship in the U.S. Navy, or an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer comes in from rough seas, Japanese shipwrights and American sailors climb under the massive steel hull shoulder to shoulder.

Through freezing winter nights and sweltering summers, Japanese welders lay down flawless steel seams that U.S. Navy inspectors call the gold standard of the Pacific.

Warships are made of steel. Alliances are kept afloat by the men with welding torches in the bottom of the dock.

yokosuka.t: October, 1989. Battleship New Jersey is part of the American battle line during a fleet exercise, followed by USS Missouri and the nuclear-powered guided missi…
yokosuka.tx:
October, 1989. Battleship New Jersey is part of the American battle line during a fleet exercise, followed by USS Missouri and the nuclear-powered guided missile cruiser USS Long Beach, with screening ships astern. The photo was taken from the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Enterprise off the coast of Yokosuka, Japan.

Ships in a formation like this one worked together, each adding its own strengths and helping to protect the others. Even a battleship with nine 16-inch guns relied on the ships around it.

Nearby ships and aircraft were tracked on board in the Combat Engagement Center. Big ships can’t turn on a dime, so knowing what was nearby mattered for coordination and safety. The CEC is one of the most restored areas on the ship and a must-see when you visit.

qt.t: JUST IN: U.S. military bans Chinese-made BYD vehicles from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, citing "unacceptable security risks."

kadena.tx:
U.S. Forces Japan(USFJ) just banned every Chinese-made BYD vehicle from Kadena Air Base, the largest U.S. air base overseas.

Starting Monday, October 26, the ban applies at all gates with zero exceptions. Personnel cars, contractor vehicles, taxis, and delivery trucks are all barred.

Base spokesperson Lt. Col. Alli Stormer said the vehicles present “an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission.” Officials cite the cameras, sensors, and real-time cloud links in modern connected EVs, which can map surroundings and transmit data from inside a sensitive installation.

Kadena hosts key Pacific air operations and the Typhon system (Tomahawk missiles that can reach Beijing). The move follows the Pentagon’s June 2026 addition of BYD to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies, alongside Alibaba, Baidu, and NIO.

Other bases are watching. When everyday cars become potential collection platforms, military sites are forced to treat them as security risks.

kadena.tx:
Since Monday, guards at every gate of Kadena Air Base on Okinawa have been turning away anything built by BYD. Private cars, contractor vans, taxis, delivery trucks. No exceptions.

The base calls the Chinese cars an unacceptable risk to its people and its mission. Think about what a BYD Sealion 7, sold in Japan, does on its own: cameras around the body stream a live 360-degree view of everything nearby. Now park it beside a flight line where F-22s and RC-135 spy planes operate. The car is the sensor.

In June the Pentagon put BYD on its list of 188 Chinese military companies, a label BYD rejects.

What I keep coming back to is that Tokyo has been building the same wall all year. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan. Beijing retaliated in January by banning dual-use exports to Japan's military. Tokyo called it absolutely unacceptable and refused to retract a word. In April it moved to restrict local-government tech purchases to state-certified products, which in practice shuts out Chinese vendors. Last week Nikkei reported a new security certification for data centers and cloud services, widely read as aimed at Chinese providers.

Beijing keeps trying to punish Japan for saying out loud what Taiwan means to its survival, and Japan keeps answering by closing doors.

BYD has been opening more showrooms in rural Japan, where trains and buses are thin. As of this week, none of those cars gets past Kadena's gates.

qt.t: OBAMA: Iran didn't have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place and I didn't have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy.

fordow.tx:
If anyone believes this nonsense, here are the facts he is counting on you not knowing.

The deal did not end Iran's nuclear program. It rented a pause. Iran kept its centrifuges, kept Fordow buried in a mountain, kept enriching to 3.67%, and the key restrictions came with expiration dates. The sunset clauses began lifting in 2025. Obama's own answer at the time was that breakout time "would have shrunk almost down to zero" as the deal expired. His deal scheduled the problem for his successors.

The regime lied its way into the deal. The JCPOA was premised on Iran coming clean about past weapons work. In 2018 Israel pulled Iran's own nuclear archive out of a Tehran warehouse: tens of thousands of documents on the Amad Project, a crash program to build nuclear weapons, preserved and hidden while Iran certified it had no such program. The IAEA later found uranium traces at undeclared sites Iran never explained.

The deal paid for terror. Sanctions relief unfroze roughly $100 billion and the US delivered $1.7 billion in cash. That money flowed to the IRGC, Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis. Diplomacy with a regime at war with you is financing, not peace.

And the result? By 2025 Iran was enriching to 60%, a short technical step from weapons grade, with enough material for multiple bombs and the IAEA declaring it in violation of its obligations. That is what required military force this year. Iran marched to the threshold under the deal's cover and after it.

"I didn't have to fire a missile" is true. He handed the regime money, legitimacy, and a timetable, and left the missiles to be fired a decade later by someone else. Appeasing a dictatorship doesn't buy peace. It buys the dictatorship time.

fordow.t: Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—t…
fordow.tx:
Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—the US military’s 30,000-pound bunker-buster, engineered to strike deeply buried and heavily fortified targets. 

Dropped by B-2 stealth bombers, the GPS-guided weapon uses its immense weight and hardened casing to penetrate underground before detonating. Its reported penetration capability reaches around 60 metres, while Fordow’s underground facilities are estimated to lie roughly 80–90 metres beneath the mountain.

That raises a critical question: can even America’s most powerful conventional bunker-buster destroy a facility buried deeper than its estimated penetration limit? The answer depends on the structure, geology and effects of the strikes—not just the bomb’s size.

Then came the strikes.

Israel began attacking Iran’s nuclear infrastructure on June 13. Nine days later, the United States launched Operation Midnight Hammer against Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan.

More than 70 weeks have now passed.

The IAEA still cannot fully account for Iran’s 60% uranium stockpile.

Before the strikes, experts assessed that Iran could potentially move from 60% to weapons-grade material in days to weeks if it retained sufficient enrichment capacity. Turning that material into an actual nuclear weapon would take considerably longer, months or potentially more than a year under current conditions.

So the question remains:
WHERE IS THE URANIUM?

How much survived?
Where is it stored?
And has Iran retained or rebuilt the capability needed to enrich it further?

More than 70 weeks after Operation Midnight Hammer, those are questions the world still needs answered.

I am the Deputy Director for Continuity of Enrichment at the Atomic Energy Organization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I would like to thank the United States Air Force and the Israeli Air Force for performing our annual asset verification.

Last June they dropped bunker-busters on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan and announced that the Islamic Republic’s key enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. I opened the shared drive the next morning. The folder still existed. Someone had renamed it “Temporary Entrance Maintenance—Peaceful Purposes.” The material we had moved the week before was listed under “Off-Site Professional Development.” I approved the rename. It auto-saved. The Supreme Leader’s fatwa against nuclear weapons was already in the folder. It has been in the folder since 2003. It has never been closed.

The fatwa is excellent documentation. It is oral. It is cited. It is never quite published as a classic ruling that would require us to stop. We present it to the IAEA. We present it to visiting ambassadors. We present it to the people who ask why the centrifuges keep turning. The fatwa covers use. The continuity plan covers everything else. Both documents are correct. One of them is temporary. The temporary one is still running.

The Atomic Energy Organization handles the public face: electricity, radiopharmaceuticals, sovereignty, service to humanity. The Organization of Defensive Innovation and Research handles the other face. The IRGC built the tunnels at Fordow because the IRGC builds tunnels. We do not discuss which face is which in the same meeting. We do not need to. The shared drive does not care which letterhead is on the folder.

In February they came back. The first wave hit the compound while the Supreme Leader was still above ground. We marked him “Out of Office—Permanent” and kept the continuity call going. The IRGC commander, the Defense Minister, and several others were marked the same way. The call continued. The new strikes were logged as incomplete because the knowledge had already been restructured around the material that survived the previous incomplete strikes. The restructuring was finished before the second round started. The second round is still listed as “In Progress.” It has been in progress for eight months. The Islamic Republic remains in the header.

Now the Space Force watches everything. They can read a name badge from orbit. We issued guidance that no one is to wear a name badge. The guidance is followed. Last week a technician arrived in a jacket that still had the old badge sewn into the lining. The satellite noted the stitching. We have opened a ticket. The ticket is currently assigned to Facilities. Facilities was struck in June. Facilities has not responded. The jacket is still in the system.

The latest American statement says there isn’t much activity at the remaining sites. Our latest report says the same thing. The two reports match. Matching reports are what we track. Activity is defined as anything that produces a useful image on the next pass. We have reduced useful images. We have not reduced the ability to produce them later. The fatwa is still in the folder. The material is still in the folder. The people who remember how the machines go together are still employed by the Islamic Republic.

I am sometimes asked if the program continues. The program continues in the form it has always continued under the Islamic Republic: residual material that was not destroyed, machines that can still be assembled, and a shared drive that survived two rounds of bunker-busters because no one thought to bomb the shared drive. None of these items require a new hall. All of them require that no one stand still long enough for the next satellite to finish spelling the name on the jacket.

My pension vests in 2029. The spring assessment is already drafted. It will state that the program has been degraded. It will also state that the degradation is measurable, tem

One Iranian voice worth watching closely at the moment is Mehdi Mohammadi, strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

- In his latest assessments, Mohammadi argues that signs of a new military confrontation, particularly between Iran and Israel, have intensified considerably and that the situation is approaching what he calls “zero hour.”

- More significantly, he believes the political decision between Trump and Netanyahu has already been made, and that the remaining problems are mainly intelligence, operational and logistical ones.

- Mohammadi’s assessments are not official statements and should not be treated as such. But they are repeatedly amplified by media and platforms close to Iran’s security establishment.

- For that reason alone, I think what he is writing at the moment deserves to be taken seriously, not necessarily as a prediction of what will happen, but as an indication of how at least part of the Iranian security environment is reading the situation.

#Iran

natanz.tx:
Earlier this summer, the wonderful editors at @thebafflermag asked me if I wanted to contribute an essay for a forthcoming issue.

I said I wanted to write about Iranian bricks.

Iran's remarkable brick architecture has become something of a meme. Everyday there's a new picture circulating online of a beautiful brick edifice in some Iranian city (often courtesy of @SustainableTall).

But why is Iran, a country dealing with so many traumas, the site of the most innovative and ambitious brick architecture in the world?

That's the question I set out to answer in this essay, which starts with a visit to the mudbrick village of Abyaneh, just over the ridge from the nuclear site at Natanz.

pickaxe.tx:
🚨Iran update, Oct 30: Major military strike appears imminent

The region is on extreme high alert right now. If you’ve seen this setup before, you know this feeling (and today, right after the markets close) something big could happen.

Here is what I think is actually coming: 

a synchronized, lightning-fast attack across the whole country at zero hour. The key difference this time is geography. In the past, operations were mostly limited to southern bases, which made covering a massive country like Iran very difficult. Now, with open corridors from the north and west through Azerbaijan and Iraq, they can cover the entire map in one single move. 

The regime will have no effective radar or air defense left to defend its underground missile cities and nuclear site ( Pickaxe mountain). 
Many people rightly believe the total destruction of the nuclear site beneath Pickaxe mountain is not possible from the air, but I think a quick, high-impact action against Pickaxe Mountain is to make a point. It’s mostly for public impact, just enough to announce that the "regime’s rising nuclear threat is neutralized again" and calm the markets and shift the geopolitical risk premium down right before Tuesday's election.

Here is the alternative: JD Vance and the team reportedly gave them an offer and an ultimatum, a last-minute deal ( something like the MoU but this time about like letting inspectors in, just to calm down the market) But I believe this regime will refuse it out of pure bad judgment. 

They are living under the illusion that by walking away, they can stop Trump from getting a political win before the election for Republicans. They don’t understand that foreign policy doesn't work like that, and they are in a complete checkmate position regardless.

They also keep underestimating the U.S. military. They measure everything based on past events, forgetting that they have never actually experienced full U.S. capability, or how fast and decisive a real strike is.

They are walking right into a massive miscalculation. On top of underestimating U.S. military power, they are convinced Trump is just bluffing and won't take bold action right before the election. That exact assumption is what makes a sudden, highly decisive strike the ultimate strategic surprise.

We’ll know very soon what they picked: a cosmetic deal, or an attack.

That warning is coming from one of Wall Street's most experienced commodity experts.

Former Goldman Sachs commodities chief Jeffrey Currie says the world is dangerously close to a crisis that could make soaring oil prices look like the least of our problems.

With reports that the U.S and Israel are considering massive strikes on Iran's leadership and energy infrastructure, the consequences of another escalation could reach far beyond the Middle East.

Because when energy supplies are disrupted, everything gets more expensive.

Diesel powers agriculture. Natural gas is essential to fertiliser production. Shipping carries food across the planet.

And all three are under increasing pressure.

Jeffrey warns that another major escalation could devastate already fragile supply chains, drive food prices higher and turbocharge social unrest.

But there's a bigger problem.

He believes the global economic order is already coming apart.

Countries are retreating from globalisation, governments are drowning in debt, and investors are increasingly turning to physical assets like gold to protect their wealth

pickaxe.tx:
🇨🇭 🇮🇷 How deep is deep enough to beat a bunker buster? About 200 meters... and Iran may already be digging there.

“There’s no, there’s no tools in any tool kit that can go and take out 200m.”

If Tehran’s nuclear work now sits that far down, the next round of strikes could end up hitting rock.

🚨🔥Just hours ago, multiple Russian Il-76 giant transport planes roared in low-altitude flight, forcibly landing at Iran's Bushehr Air Base!

But this time, the Russians aren't here to deliver gifts—they're here to "flee for their lives."

There are even reports that while the planes hurriedly picked up people, they were also frantically offloading weapons to Iran...

What on earth happened?

If you look closely at this timeline, you'll spot an utterly shocking reversal:

Just a few weeks ago, Russia's state atomic energy corporation (Rosatom) proudly announced: "We're defying the odds, arranging for personnel to return to Iran!"

By mid-October, 135 top Russian nuclear experts had already returned to Iran's only nuclear power plant—the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant—and plans were in place to ramp it up to 200.

Everything seemed to be getting back to normal.

Yet, just a few days later, the policy flipped completely overnight!

Russian military planes raced to Iran, with one goal in mind: Before the situation spirals totally out of control and full-scale military escalation erupts, urgently evacuate every last Russian nuclear expert!

Remember the last time Russia pulled off a massive emergency evacuation like this?
It was right when the war first broke out—94 people yanked out in a single day, followed by over 600 more in waves.

After finally sending those core technical personnel back, now they're using military transport planes to speed in and "rescue" them all out.

What does this mean?

1️⃣ Russia's assurances of security and expectations for the local situation have completely collapsed.
2️⃣ Moscow likely has highly precise intel: A heart-stopping major strike is about to land.
3️⃣ In a top-sensitive zone like a nuclear reactor, once the shooting starts, it could turn into a "Chernobyl-level" catastrophe—Russia absolutely won't let its own experts become cannon fodder or hostages.

From "full return" to "frantic military airlift evacuation"—all in just two or three weeks.

Before the storm hits, the slyest big birds have already flown the coop. This decision Russia made at breakneck speed is probably the most authentic signal light for where the Middle East situation is headed right now 😎💥

suez.t: On this day—October 23, 1942 An SS Einsatzkommando unit was waiting in Athens for the order to bring the Holocaust to Mandate Palestine’s Jews when British for…
suez.tx:
On this day—October 23, 1942

An SS Einsatzkommando unit was waiting in Athens for the order to bring the Holocaust to Mandate Palestine’s Jews when British forces under Montgomery opened the Second Battle of El Alamein.

By the summer of 1942, Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps had driven deep into Egypt. British forces held a defensive line at El Alamein, 60 miles west of Alexandria. From there, the road to the Suez Canal and to Mandate Palestine with nearly 600,000 Jews was open. Another 75,000 lived in Egypt, and both communities understood the danger. Reports of mass killings of Jews in Europe had already reached them.

In Berlin, an Einsatzkommando under Walther Rauff was assembled and positioned in Athens. Its orders were to carry out “special operations” against the Jewish population once Axis forces advanced beyond Egypt. Local Arabs in Mandate Palestine, anticipating a German arrival, marked Jewish houses for seizure. Grandi Mufti Amin al-Husseini had already met with Hitler and sought Arab units to fight alongside German forces against the Jews and the British.

On the night of October 23, Montgomery’s Eighth Army launched a massive artillery barrage and infantry assault. Over the following days, the Axis lines broke. Rommel’s forces began a long retreat to the west. The Einsatzkommando never deployed to Mandate Palestine, but it later operated in Tunisia.

The battle is usually remembered as a turning point in the North African campaign. For the Jews of Mandate Palestine and Egypt, it was the point at which a planned extension of the Holocaust was halted.

suez.t: October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts in…
suez.tx:
October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts into a wall of flame and thunder that can be felt in the chest from miles away. The Second Battle of El Alamein has begun. It is the battle that will finally break Rommel in the desert, the hinge of the whole war in North Africa, and the victory that Churchill would say marked "the end of the beginning."

I have been following the desert war since the early days of this series, Rommel the Desert Fox running the British ragged back and forth across Libya and Egypt, the see-saw campaign that had swung all the way to El Alamein, the last defensible line before the Nile, the Suez Canal, and the oil of the Middle East. In the summer Rommel had been stopped there, barely, in the first battle. Now the British Eighth Army had a new commander, Bernard Montgomery, a careful, methodical, supremely confident general who had rebuilt the army's morale and refused to attack until he had overwhelming strength.

And by October he had it. Montgomery had built up a crushing superiority, in men, in tanks, in guns, in aircraft, in supplies, far more than Rommel could match, because the Axis supply line across the Mediterranean was being strangled while the British were pouring reinforcements, including masses of new American-built Sherman tanks, into Egypt. Rommel himself was away sick in Germany when the blow fell, his army dug in behind vast belts of mines and wire the Germans grimly called the "Devil's Gardens."

Montgomery's plan was not clever maneuver but deliberate, grinding attrition, a battle he called "crumbling." It opened on the night of the 23rd with one of the greatest artillery bombardments since the First World War, those eight hundred-plus guns firing in a stupendous barrage that announced the offensive and smashed at the Axis positions. Then the infantry went in, in the moonlight, to clear paths through the enormous minefields so the armor could pass, and the fighting settled into a brutal, close-quarters slog through the mines and the dug-in defenses.

It was not quick. For days the battle hung in the balance, the British grinding forward yard by yard through the Devil's Gardens, taking heavy losses, the attack at times seeming to stall. Rommel rushed back from Germany to take command, but he had no answer to Montgomery's material superiority and his relentless pressure, and critically he was running out of fuel, his tanks increasingly immobilized for lack of petrol. Montgomery kept up the attrition, wearing the Axis forces down, destroying tanks he could replace and Rommel could not, until at last, in early November, he concentrated his armor and punched through.

Rommel's front broke. Against Hitler's furious orders to stand and die, Rommel, to save what was left of his army, began a long retreat westward across the desert, a withdrawal that would not stop for hundreds of miles. The Axis army in the desert had been decisively beaten for the first time, and it would never recover the initiative. Combined with the Anglo-American landings in northwest Africa that came just days later, El Alamein doomed the entire Axis position in North Africa.

The victory meant an enormous amount, and not just militarily. It was the first great, clear-cut British land victory over the Germans in the whole war, coming after years of defeats and retreats, and it was desperately needed for Allied morale. Church bells were rung in Britain to celebrate. Churchill captured its meaning in one of his famous lines: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." The tide in the west had turned, and it turned here, in the desert, beginning with those eight hundred guns firing into the dark on the night of the 23rd.

suez.t: Eritrea’s Coveted Geopolitical Location and Irreplaceable Strategic Role in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the State of Erit…
suez.tx:
Eritrea’s Coveted Geopolitical Location and Irreplaceable Strategic Role in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa

Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the State of Eritrea
Research and Documentation Division
29 October 2026

Eritrea’s location along the Red Sea and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has long made it a vital crossroads linking Africa, the Middle East, and global shipping routes. Since the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, its coastline has underpinned a major artery of international trade and energy flows. Today, as conflicts in Yemen, Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia threaten regional stability, Eritrea’s relative cohesion and independent foreign policy give it outsized importance for maritime security and regional order.

Eritrea’s strategic weight goes beyond geography. It stems from a consistent emphasis on sovereignty, resistance to external pressure, and support for littoral-state cooperation to secure the Red Sea. In a Horn of Africa marked by state fragility and competing external interests, Asmara’s posture—acknowledged by partners including Egypt, Sudan, and Somalia—positions it as a stabilizing actor whose choices affect security and commerce well beyond its borders.

suez.tx:
Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, member of Ansarallah's Supreme Political Council, criticized Saudi Arabia's claims of seeking regional de-escalation through its defense minister's visit to Tehran, arguing that Riyadh's diplomatic rhetoric contradicts its continued war, blockade, and occupation of Yemen.
——
In a statement responding to the Saudi Foreign Ministry, al-Houthi outlined the following positions:

• Riyadh cannot claim to promote regional peace and security while continuing its military attacks, blockade, and occupation of Yemen. Houthi said Saudi Arabia's actions directly contradict its stated commitment to de-escalation.

• Saudi Arabia must halt its aggression, lift the blockade, withdraw from occupied Yemeni territory, and compensate Yemen for destruction caused since 2015. He stressed that if Saudi attacks cease, Yemeni operations will also stop and normal life can resume.

• Houthi criticized the so-called 'Mecca Defense Pact', arguing that it seeks to address what its members call the Iranian crisis while concealing what he described as outright aggression against Iran. He warned that Saudi Arabia's previous alliances had failed and that Riyadh had even turned against former partners.

• He condemned Egypt and its parliament for supporting the defense of Saudi Arabia, arguing that such a position effectively amounts to declaring war on Yemen. He warned that Egypt risks repeating its military entanglement in Yemen during the 1960s, exhausting its forces and potentially leaving Sinai vulnerable to Israeli expansion and plans to displace Palestinians into Egyptian territory.

• Houthi stressed that Yemen does not fear new military alliances but warned these countries against supporting Saudi attacks, the blockade, or the occupation of Yemen. He urged them instead to direct their cooperation against Israel, which he said is waging war across Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran while also threatening Egypt.

• He rejected claims that Yemen poses a threat to regional waterways, maintaining that Yemen's position contributes to protecting Bab al-Mandab, the Suez Canal, and the wider Arab and Islamic region.

• He reaffirmed that Yemen's political and military position has remained unchanged since 2015, arguing that US, British, and Israeli intelligence agencies manufacture fears of unspecified threats to perpetuate divisions and conflict within the Arab and Islamic world.

taiwan-strait.t: What if the most revealing evidence about Nixon's position on Taiwan was never published in the 1972 Shanghai Communique? A TOP SECRET White House briefing pre…

qt.t:
48 hours before Nixon landed in China, Kissinger sent him a TOP SECRET memo.

Dated February 19, 1972, it offered a remarkably candid psychological and strategic assessment of Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai.

A few lines caught my eye:

"They see history on their side."

In the previous pages, Kissinger recognized something remarkable about China's leaders: they were deeply ideological, yet extraordinarily pragmatic. They understood the long game of history.

But Kissinger also understood something crucial: both men were in their seventies. Time was running out, and they wanted to secure their country's future before leaving the political stage.

He warned Nixon that China would judge America not merely by its words, but by its seriousness, reliability, and willingness to deliver on its commitments.

And then came his chilling final warning:

History might remember Nixon's visit as "a gallant but stillborn venture."

Nixon himself underlined numerous passages in this classified memo.

Two days later, he walked into Mao's study in Beijing's Zhongnanhai.

By the end of the visit, the two countries had issued the Shanghai Communique.

Kissinger had warned of a historic fai

taiwan-strait.tx:
What if the most revealing evidence about Nixon's position on Taiwan was never published in the 1972 Shanghai Communique?

A TOP SECRET White House briefing prepared for his historic China visit contained language far more explicit than the carefully negotiated public statement.

It said Washington would not claim Taiwan's status was undetermined. It would not encourage other countries to make that claim either.

And then there was a handwritten note:
"Taiwan will be settled."

I examined this document at the Nixon Presidential Library about a decade ago.

Now, let's uncover what this remarkable document reveals about one of the most consequential diplomatic agreements of the Cold War.

On February 28, 1972, as President Richard Nixon's historic visit to China drew to a close, Washington and Beijing issued the Shanghai Communique, the first of the three foundational joint communiques that would come to define China-US relations.

Without question, the most important part of the communique was its language on Taiwan.

The US side declared: The United States acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China and that Taiwan is a part of China. The United States Government does not challenge that position.

When I was studying US foreign policy at Cornell, I discussed this particular wording with two of my instructors. Both interpreted it as meaning that the United States had been committed to the One China principle and that Taiwan was part of China.

Yet many of Washington's subsequent actions appeared inconsistent with the language of the communique. So they viewed this as a failure by the United States to honor its commitments.

Later, however, while studying at Stanford, I heard a strikingly different interpretation from another professor. She was also a renowned fellow at Hoover and a longtime China specialist who had been reading the People's Daily (人民日报) consistently since the 1970s. And she spent most of her career researching in DC.

She pointed out that Washington's diplomats were often far more deliberate in their choice of words than most people might imagine.

And the key, she explained, lay in just two English words: Acknowledge and Recognize.

In everyday English, acknowledge can mean admitting that something is true, but it can also simply mean being aware of, taking note of, or recognizing the existence of a particular position.

In diplomatic language, however, recognize often carries a stronger implication of formal recognition.

This is why some diplomats in DC confidently claim that the United States has never broken its promises. Their argument is that acknowledge does not go as far as recognize. In their interpretation, Washington merely "heard" that the Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait maintained there was one China and that Taiwan was part of China, without formally endorsing that position as its own.

What did the White House really think about Taiwan behind closed doors? Let's take a closer look at this memo.
-- Neither of us should allow the Taiwan issue to color unduly our developing relationship. There are many areas in which cooperation between our two countries would be to our mutual benefit, and the absence of diplomatic relations due to Taiwan ought not to prevent such cooperation.

In the Legal Status of Taiwan part, A section headed "Your Position" explicitly laid out the stance President Nixon was advised to take on Taiwan.
-- You hope that the assurances which you have already given regarding our policy not to support "two Chinas," "one China, one Taiwan," or the Taiwan independence movement will convince the Chinese of your good intentions.

-- Regarding the status of Taiwan, you have noticed that Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait agree that there is only one China and that Taiwan is a part of it. In this sense we do not maintain that the status of Taiwan is undetermined. There will be no statements from US officials about Ta

taiwan-strait.t: 🛰️ CHANGING OF THE KINGS: China's TJS-17 & TJS-19 swap coverage in GEO The "Four Kings" (TJS-15, 16, 17, and 19) are classified as Chinese GEO Satellites launc…
taiwan-strait.tx:
🛰️ CHANGING OF THE KINGS: China's TJS-17 & TJS-19 swap coverage in GEO

The "Four Kings" (TJS-15, 16, 17, and 19) are classified as Chinese GEO Satellites launched in 2025 to support the PLA's SIGINT and early warning missions.

Over the past month, our team watched two of the "Four Kings" satellites trade places across 40° of the GEO belt, leaving one sitting between Yaogan 41, a GEO surveillance satellite, and a U.S. inspector, USA 270.

TJS-17 (SSC.63524), the "King of the North", held 164.5°E (above the Pacific, just west of Nauru) since Aug 2025. On 29 Sep it raised its orbit ~202 km and began drifting west at ~2.6°/day.

TJS-19 (SSC.63924), the "King of the South", held 141.3°E (above the equator north of New Guinea) since May 2025. On 7 Oct it lowered its orbit ~197 km and began drifting east at ~2.5°/day, toward the slot TJS-17 had just left. The two crossed paths on 8-9 Oct.

TJS-17 stopped its drift on 15 Oct and parked at ~123.5°E, between YAOGAN-41 (SSC.58582) at 123.2°E and GSSAP USA 270 (SSC.41744) at 125.3°E. Its new spot sits above the Molucca Sea, nearly due south of the Philippines and Taiwan.

TJS-19 reached 167.3°E and then burned again on 22 Oct to drift back west at ~0.85°/day. That's an interesting use of fuel, possibly a correction for an overshoot.

Net effect: Western-Pacific coverage at 165°E stays (TJS-19 takes over), 141°E is now empty, and TJS-17 now watches the South China Sea / Taiwan Strait from ~123°E.

A coordinated handoff or a new mission? We'll keep watching. 

#Space #GEO #China
